title: How accurately does a real keypoint detector localise features as images get noisier and blurrier?
lede: on 30 warped real photographs SIFT keypoints localise to 0.13 px per axis at zero noise and 0.32 px at noise sigma 10 grey levels, 0.59 px at 40, so sensing-ba's assumed 0.5 px sits at roughly sigma 28; large keypoints are worse, blur matters little
summary: sensing-ba and sensing-recon assumed 0.5 to 1 px of Gaussian pixel noise on every observation. This project measures it: OpenCV SIFT on ten scikit-image photographs, each warped by three random known homographies, with Gaussian noise (0 to 40 grey levels) or blur (0 to 3 px) added to both images, and the error of every ratio-passing mutual match that lands within 3 px of the truth. Per keypoint and axis, the localisation sigma is 0.13 px with no added noise (partly bilinear resampling: an integer shift gives exactly zero), 0.23 at sigma 5, 0.32 at 10, 0.43 at 20 and 0.59 at 40; through sensing-recon’s 0.0028 radii per px that is a surface error of 0.0004 to 0.0017 radii. So 0.5 px is a pessimistic input for a well-exposed image and about right for a very noisy one. Large keypoints (diameter over 16 px) are 4× worse than small ones when clean; blur of 3 px costs 1.5×. Limits: Gaussian noise rather than shot noise, synthetic warps, one detector, errors truncated at 3 px (a lower bound, 77% kept at sigma 40), not fed back into the reconstruction.
